Patient Vignette: Nadia

Nadia is a 53-year-old married woman of Middle Eastern descent who presents for therapy at the urging of her husband. She is a ship captain, a role she has held for nearly twenty years, commanding large commercial vessels across international waters. She sits upright in the chair, her posture rigid, her hands folded in her lap. She speaks with a controlled, deliberate calm, as if she is giving a report to her crew.

She begins her story not with the sea, but with the house she grew up in—a small, cramped apartment above her father’s import shop. Her father, she says, was a man of “quiet fury.” He never raised his voice, never hit her in public. But behind the closed door of her bedroom, he would come to her at night, his face a mask of disappointment. He would take off his leather belt, fold it in half, and tell her she had disgraced the family. She was seven the first time. The offense: she had spoken to a boy at the market.

Nadia describes these beatings as a ritual. She learned to anticipate them. She would lie in bed, listening to the creak of the floorboards, the sound of his footsteps approaching. She learned to make her body go still, to hold her breath, to count the seconds until it was over. She never cried. She learned that crying made it worse. She learned that the only way to survive was to become invisible, to exist in a state of perfect, silent compliance.

At eighteen, she left. She moved to a port city, worked her way up from deckhand to third mate to captain. The ship became her sanctuary. On the water, there were no walls, no closed doors. The rules were clear, the hierarchy absolute. She could control the environment. She could see the weather coming. She could prepare.

Now, at 53, she is still that seven-year-old girl. She describes a constant, low-grade vigilance. In her cabin at sea, she sleeps with her back to the wall, her door locked, a metal wrench under her pillow. She cannot tolerate anyone standing behind her. When her husband touches her shoulder unexpectedly, she flinches, sometimes with a violent start that leaves them both shaken. She has not told him why. She has never told anyone the full story.

The nightmares began in earnest about five years ago. They are not replays of the beatings. They are worse. In the dreams, she is on the bridge of her ship, and the radar goes dark. The instruments fail. The sea is smooth, but she knows something is coming from below. She cannot see it, but she feels it—a pressure, a presence. She wakes gasping, her heart pounding, convinced she is about to be hit.

Her PCL-5 score of 71 reflects the severity of her symptoms. She avoids intimacy, both emotional and physical. She has not spoken to her brother in ten years—he still lives in the old city, and the sound of his voice on the phone brings back the creak of the floorboards. She has stopped attending family gatherings, claiming her schedule is too demanding. She is hypervigilant on land. In grocery stores, she positions herself so she can see all exits. She has not sat with her back to a door in thirty years.

She tells me she is here because her husband threatened to leave. He says she is “not present.” She says she is present. She is always present. She is always watching. She is always waiting for the blow that never comes, but that she knows, with absolute certainty, is coming. She grips the armrest of the chair as she says this, her knuckles white, her eyes fixed on a point just past my shoulder. She is not afraid of me. She is afraid of the silence. In the silence, she can still hear his footsteps.
